..FOR EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA INCLUDING ORANGE...
SAN DIEGO...WESTERN RIVERSIDE AND SOUTHWESTERN SAN BERNARDINO
COUNTIES...

...FORECAST DISCUSSION UPDATE...


The low level circulation associated with Post-TS Rachel has moved
well to the north into the Mojave Desert, moving much faster than
the models anticipated. As a result, most of the strongest winds
and widespread rainfall is now behind us. West winds are still 
expected to be elevated at times for coastal and foothill areas of
San Diego County (gusting 25-35 mph), especially with showers, 
through late this morning. W/SW winds remain elevated over 
mountain ridges and desert slopes, gusting around 30-50 mph 
(locally higher) through this evening. As of 5:30 AM, another wave
of rainfall is pushing through the region. This rain is 
eventually expected to scatter out in the morning hours and become
more isolated in the afternoon (though still scattered in 
foothills and mountains).


...DISCUSSION FROM 10 PM YESTERDAY...

Post-TS Rachel is now fully embedded within the upper 
level trough and the rainfall core, out ahead of the core, is 
actively decoupling with the low level circulation. As of 9PM, the 
rainfall core has moved into southern San Diego County and winds are 
increasing out of the east along the higher SD Co. coast facing 
slopes with gusts 25-50 mph. Farther east into Imperial County, 
clusters of thunderstorms are forming in a CAPE environment of 500-
1000 J/kg. These thunderstorms have the potential to move into the 
Coachella Valley and desert slopes through around 2 AM yielding to 
rain rates above 0.50"/hr and thus increased risk for urban and 
flash flooding. 

By around 2 AM, the most widespread heavy rain bands start moving 
through the region from south to north. Models indicate widespread 
rain rates across all lower elevation areas of 0.2-0.5"/hr with 
pockets of more intense rain possibly over 1"/hr through mid-morning 
(~8-11AM). Areas receiving such rain rates are at an increased risk 
for urban and flash flooding; remain alert and heed advice of local 
officials. Simultaneously, northerly winds west of the foothills 
will increase throughout the night, gusting 15-35 mph (highest at 
the coast) through around 3-5AM Sunday. Easterly winds over the 
coastal foothills through the desert slopes will also increase 
significantly over the next several hours, from south to north, with 
wind gusts 45-65 mph, locally to 75 mph through passes and exposed 
ridges.

The strongest winds move through around 4/5 AM through 10 AM through 
SD County (~7AM-12PM for northern areas) as Post-TS Rachel makes a 
close approach. Wind gusts will increase to 25-45 mph across lower 
elevations and winds abruptly turn westerly and increase even more 
over the mountains, passes and desert slopes with gusts 50-80 mph 
(locally higher). By the afternoon, Post-TS Rachel will have moved 
north out of the region very fast. Precipitation scatters to showers 
across the lower elevations with more persistent (though weakening) 
showers and wind over the foothills and mountains for a few hours 
longer (through ~2-4PM). By evening, winds will be significantly 
reduced everywhere. Isolated showers continue for lower elevations, 
remaining scattered over the foothills/mountains through Monday 
morning. During the day Monday, the trough axis moves through, 
bringing a much more traditional round of light rainfall of around 
0.05-0.25" through the coastal basin, with higher amounts in the 
mountains (light snow above ~8,000 feet) and rain shadowing the 
deserts (less than 0.05" and breezy downslope winds). Shower 
activity looks to persist until Tuesday morning before clearing out 
Tuesday afternoon.

As conditions clear out, morning temperatures Tues/Wed will drop 
noticeably inland into the low 50s/upper 40s and in the mountain 
valleys down into the low 30s and 20s. 

High temperatures steadily rebound, returning to 80s across the 
lower elevation by Thursday and possibly into the 90s for coastal 
areas Fri/Sat courtesy of offshore winds.
